games.explanation: The market is treating this like Schlittler is the safer arm just because his ERA is prettier, but the underlying profile says he's a righty who gives up hard contact and issues too many free passes to be a road favorite. Toronto happens to run out the exact bats that punish that mistake, with Guerrero and Springer both posting xwOBAs north of .390 against right-handed pitching. Schlittler's barrel rate against righties is nearly ten percent, which is the kind of number that turns a closed-roof night at the Rogers Centre into a problem. Woods Richardson doesn't need to be brilliant, he just needs to keep pace in a game the board has already conceded. At +158 on the better Elo team at home, you're getting paid to bet the coin flip.

San Diego is the far better team getting a plus price because the market can't get past the "road dog in Cleveland" framing. Elo has the Padres 210 points clear of the Guardians, which is the kind of gap you usually see in September when a contender rolls into a tanker's yard. Vasquez isn't a great arm, but Cleveland's lineup outside of Ramirez doesn't punish mediocre command the way San Diego's does, and Tatis and Machado are both sitting north of a .355 xwOBA against right-handed pitching this year. At +111, you're getting the stronger roster, the deeper lineup, and a coin-flip price on a game that isn't a coin flip.

Emerson Hancock is the kind of arm that looks fine in the aggregate and falls apart the moment you check who he's actually facing tonight. Houston runs out Alvarez and a lineup built to punish exactly this profile, and Hancock's split against lefties (a .391 xwOBA with a double-digit walk rate) is the tell. Wesneski isn't a star, but he misses more bats than his counterpart and doesn't give the free passes back, which is how you win a game the sims already have as a coin flip. Getting the better team, the better starter, and the better matchup at -116 is the whole argument.

Luzardo is a completely different pitcher against lefties than righties, and the Twins happen to run out a lineup full of the exact bats that give him trouble. Buxton, Jeffers, and Martin all hit right-handed and have been substantially better against southpaws, which matters because Luzardo's numbers versus righties (a .304 xwOBA and a walk rate pushing nine percent) look nothing like the video-game line he posts against lefties. This is essentially a coin flip game between two evenly matched teams, with the sim landing on a one-run margin, and Minnesota is being priced like the clear underdog. +143 on the side with the platoon advantage in a projected low-scoring fight is the entire pitch.
